prompt: rgb.jpg is a horizontal strip of 5 frames, left to right in time order, sampled from the few seconds of a head-mounted (egocentric) video; the camera wearer is the viewpoint. depth.jpg, segmentation.jpg and pose.jpg are the same 5 frames rendered as a monocular depth map (brighter = nearer to the camera wearer), an instance segmentation map (coloured masks with class labels), and a body/hand skeleton map (yellow = body, magenta = hands) on black. Look at all four images. For EACH of the three maps, describe the spatial understanding that map supports, using the RGB strip for context: the layout of the scene; which people and objects are present and roughly how far each is from the camera wearer (in metres) and from each other; relative positions (left/right/in front/behind, above/below); which way people face and whether they look toward the camera wearer; what is within arm's reach of the camera wearer or of others; occlusions and anything partly out of view; and how these change across the 5 frames (approach, retreat, turning). Say what each map shows that is hard to see in the RGB alone, and where the map looks unreliable. Describe only spatial facts. Do not guess anyone's intentions, social norms, or what anyone should do. Return only JSON: {"depth": "...", "segmentation": "...", "pose": "..."} with 3-5 sentences each.

descriptions.depth: The depth map separates nearby foam or mattress stacks, generally about 0.5–2 m from the camera wearer, from the open aisle and rear warehouse area, roughly 5–15+ m away; the floor lies below, the ceiling above, and the largest stacks flank the travel path. Across the five frames, nearby stacks shift from the front-left and front-right toward the left edge or out of view as the wearer moves or turns, while the open floor becomes more prominent ahead and to the left. The few people and equipment visible in the RGB appear several metres away, approximately 6–12 m, with no person clearly within arm’s reach or close enough to determine mutual spacing precisely. This map makes foreground clearance and large-scale depth ordering clearer than RGB, but broad smooth gradients, blurred boundaries, and similar brightness across some distant surfaces make metric distances, thin objects, people, and occlusions unreliable.
descriptions.segmentation: The segmentation map isolates a few small person-like regions several metres in front of the wearer and several object regions mostly along the right side in the later frames, helping distinguish separate instances and their left-right spacing against the cluttered warehouse. It also marks large regions partly outside the left edge in the first frame, showing that nearby objects are strongly cropped and occlude whatever lies behind them. Across the sequence, detected people remain small and distant rather than entering arm’s reach, while the right-side detected objects become more numerous and clustered as that part of the scene comes into view; facing direction, gaze, above/below relationships, and approach versus retreat cannot be resolved from these tiny masks. The map is highly unreliable here: large foam stacks are labelled “bed,” small equipment or materials are repeatedly labelled “suitcase,” one label appears as “pipe,” many obvious stacks are omitted, and several masks do not align cleanly with RGB boundaries.
descriptions.pose: The pose map is entirely black in all five frames, so it provides no detected body or hand skeletons and supports no direct estimate of posture, facing direction, gaze, interpersonal orientation, or reach. Using the RGB only for context, any people are small and several metres ahead, while nearby foam stacks occupy the sides of the aisle and sometimes extend partly out of frame. No change in body position, approach, retreat, or turning can be measured from this map across the sequence, and it cannot reveal occluded limbs or hands that are difficult to see in RGB. Its blank output is therefore unreliable as evidence that no people or hands are present; it most likely reflects failed or absent pose detections at this scale.
